content: The document provides updated guidelines for assessing and managing children at primary health-care facilities to prevent overweight and obesity, particularly in the context of the double burden of malnutrition. These updates are part of the Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) framework, which aims to address both undernutrition and the rising prevalence of childhood overweight and obesity. The guidelines emphasize the importance of anthropometric assessments, nutritional counseling, and evidence-based interventions to mitigate the risks of malnutrition in all its forms. The World Health Organization (WHO) developed these recommendations following a rigorous process outlined in its handbook for guideline development. This process included identifying priority questions, retrieving and assessing evidence, synthesizing findings, and formulating recommendations. The guidelines aim to support health-care providers, policymakers, and program managers in making informed decisions to improve child health outcomes. The document highlights the global epidemic of childhood obesity, which coexists with undernutrition in many regions. In 2016, 155 million children were stunted, 52 million were wasted, and 41 million were overweight. Both undernutrition and obesity are associated with increased risks of morbidity, mortality, and impaired development. Paradoxically, children with a history of low birth weight or stunting are at higher risk of becoming overweight or obese later in life, which increases their likelihood of developing cardiovascular disease or diabetes. The guidelines also address the need for health workers to be equipped with tools and training to provide effective nutritional counseling. This includes promoting appropriate infant and young child feeding practices to prevent both undernutrition and obesity. The IMCI framework, traditionally focused on undernutrition, is being expanded to include guidance on preventing childhood obesity and promoting health. The recommendations are intended to help countries and their partners implement evidence-based strategies to assess and manage children at primary health-care facilities. This includes settings where both undernutrition and obesity are prevalent. The guidelines also aim to contribute to achieving global health targets, such as the Sustainable Development Goals and the WHO Global Strategy for Women’s, Children’s, and Adolescents’ Health. The document outlines specific areas of focus, including: 1. Anthropometric assessment and classification of nutritional status in children. 2. Management of acute or chronic malnutrition in children. 3. Management of children who are overweight or obese. The primary audience for these guidelines includes national policymakers, development partners, program managers, health-care providers, researchers, and clinicians. The recommendations are designed to be practical and actionable, supporting efforts to improve child health and nutrition globally.
